description: A Astro Health BR reúne cinco graduandos da Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU), sendo Ciência da Computação, Sistemas de Informação e Medicina. Unindo competências em desenvolvimento full-stack, análise de dados, arquitetura de software e telemetria, a equipe projetou e implementou uma solução autônoma de monitoramento biomédico e suporte à decisão clínica para astronautas em missões de espaço profundo durante o NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
summary:
Astro Health BR has developed a prototype for an intuitive platform designed to monitor the health of astronauts on missions to Mars. During long-duration space travel, the crew faces extreme isolation, communication delays with Earth, and unprecedented physiological stressors—making rapid, independent access to medical support essential.
Our prototype addresses this challenge by centralizing real-time biometric tracking into a clear, adaptable dashboard. In addition to presenting vital signs in an accessible format, the system provides actionable protocols and instructions tailored to each phase of the mission, ensuring that astronauts can identify anomalies early and act with precision, even millions of miles away.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

AstroHealth Monitor is an onboard health decision-support dashboard built to answer one critical question during spaceflight: "What do I do now, and why?" It tracks each crew member day by day and hour by hour across three mission phases: Orbital Station, Transit to Mars, and Mars Base.

At its core, a deterministic rules engine performs personal baseline triage by evaluating daily biomarkers and logs—including blood pressure, resting heart rate, glucose, body temperature, sleep, mood, resistance training, cumulative radiation, and neuro-ocular symptoms—against each astronaut's own baseline and a 7-day rolling window. Based on these comparisons, the system classifies each day as Normal, Warning, or Critical and identifies the affected physiological domain (cardiovascular, immune, metabolic, neuro-ocular, behavioral, musculoskeletal, or radiation). Alongside daily tracking, a simulated smartwatch streams continuous hourly telemetry (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, SpO2, HRV, and stress) that evolves dynamically from hour to hour in response to logged pain, applied countermeasures, and accumulated fatigue.

These data streams feed into a 0–100 cumulative readiness model that starts from the day's baseline condition, depletes as physiological strain accumulates, and recovers exponentially during sleep, rest, and countermeasures. Regardless of the numerical readiness score, explicit safety rules automatically cap or suspend Extravehicular Activity (EVA) whenever critical conditions such as fever, hypoxia, severe pain, or a critical alert are detected. On alert days, a decision-first interface immediately surfaces "Today's Decision," presenting what happened, the recommended action, and the exact measurements triggering the alert side by side with the astronaut's personal baseline, while an alert pop-up mirrors the same guidance so crew members never have to search for next steps.

Crew members also interact with an anatomical body map that highlights affected organs on front and back views with concise clinical explanations, while allowing astronauts to click any of 15 body regions to report discomfort type and intensity directly into the readiness and triage models. When an alert occurs, an AI copilot receives a compact telemetry summary to explain in plain language why the physiological change happens in spaceflight, recommend countermeasures, and indicate whether the case can be managed onboard or requires escalation to flight surgeons on Earth; if connectivity is lost, a local deterministic engine generates the exact same structured guidance offline. Additionally, a predictive trend panel flags gradual multi-day deterioration before it becomes an active alert (treating radiation as a cumulative mission dose), a data-quality panel recommends follow-up exams when telemetry is missing or inconclusive, and daily missions, experience points (XP), and an exercise coach support adherence to the 60-minute daily resistance training protocol.

BENEFITS

AstroHealth Monitor provides true onboard autonomy during deep-space missions where one-way communication delays to Mars can reach approximately 20 minutes, giving crews immediate, explained clinical guidance without waiting for ground support. By evaluating changes against each astronaut's personal baseline rather than generic population averages, it delivers individualized precision while maintaining clarity under high stress through a single unified status, one clear action, and consistent evidence across every screen. Its offline-first design ensures resilience when external AI services or Earth communications are unavailable, while predictive trend tracking and data-quality alerts catch emerging risks and diagnostic gaps before they escalate into medical emergencies.

INTENDED IMPACT

The project aims to shorten the loop between a physiological deviation and an informed, timely action on long-duration space missions, making complex biomedical telemetry actionable for non-physician crew members. Beyond spaceflight, this offline-first, baseline-driven approach translates directly to remote and austere environments on Earth, including Antarctic research stations, maritime vessels, offshore oil platforms, low-connectivity rural telemedicine, and home monitoring of chronic conditions.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

The backend was developed in Python using FastAPI, pandas, and NumPy, supported by a structured Excel (.xlsx) mission dataset. The frontend was built with TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Recharts, and Lucide icons. Clinical synthesis relies on the Groq API (model openai/gpt-oss-120b) configured with a system prompt grounded in NASA Human Research Program (HRP) and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) references, paired with response caching and a 3.5-second timeout before falling back to the local deterministic engine. Python with OpenCV and Pillow was used for image processing to segment and generate the 15 interactive body map regions. No physical hardware was used, as the wearable device and hourly sensor stream are simulated entirely in software.

CREATIVE ASPECT

AstroHealth Monitor combines a phase-adaptive mission-control interface—whose color palette and ambient background shift dynamically between Orbital Station, Transit to Mars, and Mars Base—with a readiness model that behaves like a living physiological system, wearing down under cumulative strain and recovering hour by hour during sleep and countermeasures so astronauts can see the direct impact of their actions. Its adaptive decision-first layout prioritizes clinical guidance and baseline evidence ahead of gamification on alert days while bringing daily missions, exercise goals, and XP forward on routine days, complemented by a dual-purpose anatomical body map that serves simultaneously as an alert display and a low-friction symptom reporting interface.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

The team designed the triage categories, cumulative tracking, and countermeasure protocols around the five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile closed environments. To account for communication latency and signal loss, the system follows an offline-first architecture in which cloud AI enhances plain-language synthesis rather than acting as a single point of failure. Clinical safety and interface consistency were prioritized by governing EVA eligibility with explicit rules, aligning the top status bar, protocol view, and alert pop-ups, and explicitly displaying an "Unknown" health status rather than "No Alert" whenever telemetry is missing. To prevent alarm fatigue, pop-ups appear only when clinical status changes rather than while browsing past mission days. Finally, the team ensured full transparency and accessibility by disclosing that all datasets are simulated and thresholds require medical validation (explicitly stating the app is a prototype rather than a certified medical device), clearly labeling all AI-generated assets in the interface (astronaut portraits, background videos, logo artwork, and LLM-written guidance), spelling out technical acronyms like Extravehicular Activity (EVA) on first use, and designing responsive layouts for desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.
